# The Light-Leak

The camera arrived in a shoebox lined with newspaper, smelling of cedar and dust. My neighbor Mrs. Okafor pressed it into my hands on the morning of the Maple Street Block Party like she was handing over a sleeping infant.

"It was my husband's," she said. "A Yashica Mat, twin-lens reflex. He photographed every wedding in this neighborhood for thirty years. Nobody's touched it since 2011."

I had volunteered to document the event because I was the only person on the organizing committee who owned anything other than a phone. What I actually owned was a five-year-old DSLR with a cracked lens cap, but when Mrs. Okafor heard about my assignment, she appeared at my door with the shoebox before I could even mention it.

"You look down into it," she explained, miming a waist-level viewfinder with her hands. "Like a well. You'll see."

I spent the morning learning the camera's weight. It was heavier than it looked, all metal and glass, with a crank that advanced the film with a sound like a small decision being made. The light meter didn't work, so I downloaded an app on my phone and carried both devices like a translator and her
